--- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.degrees()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Get degree for all nodes in the graph. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.degrees()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Get degree for all nodes in the graph. title: >- [Graph.degrees()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: Get degree for all nodes in the graph. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Get degree for all nodes in the graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L54503-L54643){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.degrees( attr_name=None, return_dict=False, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Degree of every node](../assets/graphs/degrees.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A seven-node graph, a strip of three triangles A to E with a tail F, G, each node shaded by its degree. Hub C has the most neighbors and the darkest shading, and the table lists C 4, then B, D, E 3, A, F 2, and G 1." width="100%"} For directed graphs, returns total degree (in-degree + out-degree). For undirected graphs, returns the number of neighbors. This batch method computes `get_degree()` for every node in one call and automatically stores results in the node DataFrame. Degree is the simplest measure of how connected a node is. It is useful for: - spotting hubs and poorly connected nodes at a glance - storing degree as a node attribute so it can drive later steps, such as sizing or coloring nodes in a plot or filtering with `select_nodes()` - a quick baseline before reaching for more expensive centrality measures More precisely, a node's degree here is its number of incident edges: parallel edges each count, and in undirected graphs a self-loop counts twice. Edge weights are ignored (each edge counts as `1`). For in- or out-degree alone, use `get_in_degree()` or `get_out_degree()`. With `return_dict=False` the degrees are written to the node DataFrame; with `return_dict=True` they are only returned. Note that `get_node_df()` always ends with a live `degree` column, so with the default `attr_name=` the stored attribute appears under that same column name; pick another `attr_name=` if you want a separate snapshot column. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [attr_name]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Column name to store degree values in the node DataFrame. If `None` (default), automatically uses `degree`. Overwrites column if it already exists. [return_dict]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, returns a dictionary mapping node IDs to degrees without writing anything to the graph. If `False` (default), stores in NDF and returns self for chaining. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Union[dict[int, int], Graph]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_dict=` is `True`: dictionary mapping node IDs to degree values. If `return_dict=` is `False` (default): returns self for method chaining. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~get_degree`) : The degree of a single node. [](`~degree_distribution`) : How many nodes have each degree. [](`~degree_centrality`) : Degree divided by the largest possible, for comparing graphs. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A node's degree is its number of edges. "A" is joined to both other nodes, and "B" and "C" to one each. With `return_dict=True` the degrees come back keyed by node ID, and "A" is node `1`: ::: {#e80983fd .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph.from_edges([("A", "B"), ("A", "C")]) dict(sorted(graph.degrees(return_dict=True).items())) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {1: 2, 2: 1, 3: 1} ``` ::: ::: In a directed graph, edges in and out are added together. "A" only sends edges and "C" only receives them, but all three nodes have degree `2`: ::: {#f27334f2 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} directed = ec.Graph.from_edges( [("A", "B"), ("A", "C"), ("B", "C")], directed=True ) dict(sorted(directed.degrees(return_dict=True).items())) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` {1: 2, 2: 2, 3: 2} ``` ::: ::: ### Who appears with whom In the Les Misérables network, two characters are joined when they appear in the same chapter, so a character's degree is the number of others they meet. Valjean meets 36, far more than anyone else: ::: {#261b0f9b .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} novel = ec.les_miserables() met = novel.degrees(return_dict=True) top = sorted(met, key=met.get, reverse=True)[:5] [(novel.get_label_from_id(v), met[v]) for v in top] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` [('Valjean', 36), ('Gavroche', 22), ('Marius', 19), ('Javert', 17), ('Thenardier', 16)] ``` ::: ::: The node DataFrame always has a live `degree` column that follows every edit, so storing the degrees under another name keeps a snapshot. Here they're stored as `"met"` before Valjean is taken out of the story. The layout is computed first, so that the drawings below put every character in the same place: ::: {#5522cbae .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} novel.layout_kamada_kawai() novel.degrees(attr_name="met") novel.plot( layout="pos", size_by="met", color_by="met", color_scale="sequential", show_labels=False, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: Without Valjean, everyone he met has one fewer, and 5 characters, who appear with no one else, are left with none: ::: {#1e6fcd86 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} import polars as pl novel.delete_node("Valjean") alone = novel.get_node_df().filter(pl.col("degree") == 0) alone.select("label", "met", "degree") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
